title: Low breakdown field and high ionization index in ReSe_2 avalanche field-effect transistors

paper_content.abstract:
Avalanche field-effect transistors (AFETs) based on two-dimensional (2D) materials have attracted
growing interest in optoelectronics due to their enhanced performance via carrier multiplication and their
potential applications in nanoelectronics. However, most AFETs employing 2D materials face challenges
with high breakdown fields and low ionization indexes, which limit their applications in optoelectronics.
Here, we report a ReSe -based AFET that achieves a breakdown electric field down to 2.55 kV/cm and
2
an ionization index up to 38.79. This performance is attributed to using anisotropic ReSe as the channel
2
material, which reduces unnecessary carrier collisions. Moreover, the incorporation of HfZrO as the
2
dielectric enhances gate modulation, which further mitigates scattering effects. The underlying
mechanism is validated through calculations of electron effective masses along both in- and out-of-plane
directions. Moreover, scattering probability within ReSe based on simulation model and experimental
2
data further corroborates the proposed mechanism. As a demonstration, ReSe avalanche phototransistors
2
with a high responsivity of 1.71×104 A/W and a high gain of 173 are realized based on this platform. By
incorporating anisotropic 2D materials and high-k dielectric with less carrier scattering, this AFET design
provides a promising pathway for developing high-performance avalanche photodetectors.
paper_content.introduction:
The phenomenon of avalanche multiplication has been extensively studied in optoelectronics due to its
potential to enhance optical performance through carrier multiplication1,2. Avalanche photodetectors,
which leverages this phenomenon, have attracted significant research interest in various fields including
optical communications3, biomedical imaging4, and sensing5. For these applications, it is critical for
avalanche devices to operate at low bias voltages and room temperature. However, conventional
avalanche devices made from bulk materials including Si, Ge and III-V compound often face limitations,
such as high threshold breakdown field (E ) and low ionization index (n)6,7 due to huge waste of energy
b
induced by scattering.

To overcome these challenges, two-dimensional (2D) materials8-10 have emerged as promising candidates
for low-bias avalanche devices due to their atomically thin structures11,12. Among these materials,
transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have shown great potential for high-performance devices.
TMDs can be classified based on their crystal symmetry13, including highly symmetrical hexagonal TMDs
such as MoX and WX (with X =S, Se)14,15, as well as anisotropic TMD with low-symmetry crystal
2 2
structures such as MX (M = Re, Pd; X = S, Se)16. For symmetric TMDs, tailored device architectures
2
have been utilized to enhance electric-field efficiency, thereby enabling a lower avalanche threshold
voltage17. Complementarily, minimizing energy losses from carrier scattering provides an additional and
equally important pathway to reduce the avalanche breakdown voltage.

The anisotropic TMDs show less scattering due to much weaker interlayer interactions compared to
symmetrical TMDs, which results from their distorted 1T diamond-chain structures18,19. This property
reduces scattering probability by restricting charge transport along the out-of-plane direction in the
channel20. Consequently, the carriers are apt to gain sufficient kinetic energy to trigger impact ionization
under low electric fields with minimal energy losses from scattering19. Therefore, the unique
characteristics of anisotropic TMDs make them ideal for designing avalanche devices with low E and
b
high n. Among anisotropic TMDs, ReSe is particularly promising for optoelectronic applications due to
2
its favorable optical properties21,22. However, despite its potential, the integration of ReSe in avalanche
2
devices has not yet been demonstrated.

On the other hand, the E can be modulated by gate voltage, making the choice of the dielectric layer
b
which affects gate modulation, a key factor in determining the E of avalanche devices. Pioneering works
b
utilized low-k materials like silicon dioxide (SiO )19,23 or boron nitride24 as dielectrics, which enabled
2
modulation but at the expense of high E .
b

To address these challenges, we propose an avalanche field-effect transistor (AFET) design utilizing
ReSe as the channel material and high-k HfZrO (HZO) as the dielectric. This design achieves both one
2 2
of the lowest E and one of the highest n among other reported AFETs based on 2D materials. The superior
b
performance arises from minimizing scattering energy losses due to the unique anisotropic carrier
transport of ReSe , combined with effective gate modulation due to high-k HZO dielectric. We further
2
explore the underlying mechanism behind the high breakdown performance by calculating the electron
effective mass (m*) along different crystallographic directions and the scattering probability from
experimental and theoretical aspects within ReSe . Furthermore, we demonstrate a ReSe -based avalanche
2 2
phototransistor (APT) with highly competitive characteristics built on this AFET structure. This work
underscores significance and potential of anisotropic 2D materials and high-k dielectrics in advancing
avalanche optoelectronics.

paper_content.methods:
Device fabrication.
The fabrication process of the AFET began with the atomic layer deposition of an 8-nm HZO layer onto
a heavily doped Si substrate at a temperature of 250 ˚C. Following this, ReSe flakes were mechanically
2
exfoliated from bulk ReSe crystals (obtained from HQ Graphene Supplies) and transferred onto the
2
substrate using a poly (methyl methacrylate) (PMMA)-assisted method, as depicted in Figure S1.
Subsequently, a 25-nm Ni layer was then deposited via electron-beam evaporation at a controlled low rate
of 0.1 Å/s to ensure good contact with the thin ReSe layer, and subsequently patterned through a lift-off
2
process to serve as the source/drain electrodes.

Material and device characterization.
The thickness of the ReSe materials was measured using an atomic force microscopy (NX 20 AFM, Park
2
Systems). Raman spectra were collected with a Raman microscope system utilizing a 532 nm with laser.
Electrical characterization of the avalanche device was performed using an Agilent B1500A
semiconductor analyzer at room temperature. The photonic characteristics of the FET were measured
under illumination at a wavelength of 520 nm, with the light spot diameter on the FET channel measuring
10 mm. Low-temperature FET mobility measurements were carried out from a AFET with a 285-nm SiO
2
as dielectrics using a low-frequency SR860 lock-in amplifier (Stanford Research Systems) to ensure high
sensitivity and stability. The response time measurement was performed using a voltage-probing setup.
First, the device was mounted on a PCB in series with a load resistor for current-to-voltage (I-V)
conversion. Then, the resulting voltage signal was transmitted to a KEYSIGHT MXR608A oscilloscope
using a low-noise voltage probe for capture and analysis.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The author reported a Low breakdown field and high ionization index in ReSe2 avalanche field-effect transistors. The
avalanche breakdown voltage of the device can be as low as around 4 V and the avalanche electric field can be as low as
2.55 KV/cm.The avalanche detectivity, avalanche photoresponsivity, and avalanche gain can achieve 1.71×104 A/W,
1.99×1013 Jones, and 173, respectively. Although the innovation of the article needs to be considered, there is no doubt that
the performance of the devices is great. In my opinion, this paper can be published once the following concerns can be
well addressed.
1.Please provide a detailed list of the innovative points in your article.
2.In the fifth page of your article, you said that “The threshold voltage values, extracted from the transfer curves at different
drain voltages (Vds) are consistently 0.2 V, indicating an absence of drain-indicated barrier lowering (DIBL) in this ReSe2
FET.” Could you please to introduce how you determine the turn-on voltage of the device?
3.A larger effective mass in the c-axis direction means that the migration of charge carriers between different material layers
is hindered, so charge carriers’ migration within the plane dominates, forming a pathway for charge carrier to migrate in the
material, which can effectively reduce collision scattering between charge carriers. But a larger effective mass means lower
mobility, and the effective mass of electrons in the a-axis and b-axis directions (relative to MoS2 material) is actually higher.
Can we conclude that the excellent performance of the material is due to the difference in effective mass only by analyzing
the size of the c-axis electron effective mass?
4.In avalanche breakdown, when the drain voltage exceeds the breakdown voltage, the current will increase rapidly, often
exponentially. If you were to plot the current on a logarithmic (log10) scale versus the drain voltage, you would observe a
sharp, nearly vertical rise in current as the voltage approaches and exceeds the breakdown voltage. This can more
intuitively illustrate that the current jump observed in the article is an avalanche phenomenon.
5.The article provides many proofs about the avalanche phenomenon of devices. If you have such conditions, please test
the variation of avalanche voltage with temperature. This is a more direct way to prove the avalanche phenomenon.
6.Could you please to explain how the avalanche voltage is selected and why do you choose the parameter at the
avalanche point to calculate your avalanche gain?
7.Could you please to introduce the testing method for Figure 3a in the supplementary material and explain why the current
decrease sharply at the avalanche point?
8.Why does the drain voltage required for avalanche significantly increase after replacing the HZO with SiO2 as shown in
Fig 4b in the supplementary material?
9.Is this phenomenon reliable? Could you please to repeat the measurement of several such devices to determine the
reliability of this experimental phenomenon？

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors report a room temperature low breakdown voltage (~5V) in ReSe2 device and associate it with the avalanche
process. The intrinsic anisotropic crystal structure is believed to lower the charge carrier scattering and contribute to the
phenomenon. DFT simulations were performed to extract the electron mass in a, b and c axis. The electron mass of c axis
(out of plane) is 3.5 times larger than that of a axis (in plane) and is believed as the origin of low charge carrier scattering
probability and low breakdown voltage. Finally, the photoresponse of the ReSe2 device was measured. A responsivity of
1.71×104 A/W and a gain of 173 are reported.
After carefully going through the manuscript, I personally cannot support the publication of it in the highest rated
multidisciplinary journal “Nature Communications”. My questions/queries are listed as follows.
1. There will be more than 4 orders of magnitude increase of current after breakdown. However, the IV curves are all plotted
in linear coordinate in this work. This is not a rigorous and acceptable way to show the current boost of breakdown. Please
find the IV plot in silicon and InGaAs avalanche photodiode (Optical and Quantum Electronics 52 (2020): 1-9; Nature
Communications 15, 3639 (2024), graphene/silicon and WSe2 impact ionization field-effect transistor (Nat Commun 15,
9038 (2024); Nat Commun 13, 6076 (2022))
2. As is well documented in the textbook, the current break-down could arise from either avalanche or Zener process. There
is a simple way to distinguish them from each other. Generally, the avalanche process is featured by a positive temperature
coefficient of the breakdown voltage (low temperature would freeze the lattice vibration, and thus lead to low frequency of
electron-phonon scattering), while the Zener process is featured by a negative coefficient (low temperature would increase
the bandgap and thus suppress the band to band tunneling). However, there is no such evidence present in this work.
Based on the above questions/queries, I cannot support the judgement that the current boast observed in this work is
breakdown and associate with the avalanche process.
3. To calculate the detectivity of the device, the noise is estimated as 2qIds. This is not rigorous and usually overestimates
the device performance. The noise should be measured experimentally by the standard measurement method (Nature 542,
324–327 (2017)).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
From this work, the authors present a comprehensive study on ReSe2-based avalanche field-effect transistors, claiming a record-low breakdown field (2.55 kV/cm) and a high ionization index (38.79) among reported 2D-material AFETs. These achievements are attributed to the anisotropic properties of ReSe2 and the incorporation of high-k HZO dielectric. The study also demonstrates the potential of this design through the fabrication of high-performance avalanche phototransistors. The paper is potentially interesting to the community but I believe that the manuscript may contain incomplete supporting evidence for the high performance metrics as they promote in the manuscript. Therefore, considering a high standard set in Nature Communications, I recommend that the manuscript to undergo major revisions after considering the following concerns:
1. Mechanism for the low breakdown field: while the authors attribute the low breakdown field and high ionization index to anisotropic ReSe2 properties and effective gate modulation, the quantitative relationship between these factors is not clearly established. The manuscript should provide more detailed modeling or theoretical analysis to link the observed device characteristics to the proposed mechanisms, particularly concerning the reduction in carrier scattering. I would like to suggest the following aspects to be included in their work:
a. Experimental evidence for reduction in carrier scattering at different regimes of gate voltages: mobility, carrier lifetime, etc.
b. Detailed modeling or theoretical analysis to link the observed carrier multiplication to the proposed mechanisms, particularly quantitatively linking the experimental the reduction in carrier scattering to the theoretical work.
c. Detailed description of device operation:

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In the revised manuscript, the authors have incorporated several important additions, including an analysis of the temperature coefficient, logarithmic-scale I -V
ds ds
characteristics, and corrections to the previously inaccurate detectivity calculations. These improvements have undoubtedly enhanced the overall quality of the work. However, I remain concerned about certain aspects of the newly presented data, particularly regarding the temperature coefficient and avalanche mechanism. If not addressed meticulously, these issues could lead to significant misinterpretations and critical errors in the interpretation of the results. Given these unresolved concerns, I am unable to recommend acceptance of this manuscript in its current form for publication in Nature Communications. Below, I outline specific suggestions for further clarification and refinement:
1. Temperature coefficient. The authors have supplemented their manuscript with experimental data characterizing the breakdown voltage across a temperature range of 300 K to 160 K, as presented in Supplementary Figures 3d and 3e. While this additional data provides valuable insights into the device’s thermal behavior, two critical questions emerge:
1) With the decrease in temperature, both scattering and thermal excitation effects in semiconductor (including ReSe2 FET in this work) should be suppressed, leading to an expected reduction in dark current. The current-voltage characteristics presented here should follow the conventional behavior observed in avalanche photodiodes, as extensively documented in prior literature (Nature Photonics 2020, 14, 559-563). However, the authors observed a completely opposite experimental phenomenon. In the provided figures (Supplementary Fig. 3d), the dark current in the linear region actually increased with rising temperature, growing from approximately 3*1e-10 A at 300 K to about 9*1e-10 A at 160 K. This finding is difficult to reconcile with the current theoretical framework. The authors are requested to provide a rigorous explanation for this observation.
2) Why does the breakdown voltage drop sharply from approximately 2 V to 1.4 V when the temperature changes from 300 K to 280 K (only a 20 K variation), while further decreases in temperature result in much less pronounced changes in breakdown voltage, even showing a trend toward saturation? Considering these issues, I believe the authors should include more temperature-point data, particularly in the range from 300 K to 280 K, as well as extend testing to lower temperatures (e.g., 77 K), in order to provide a more detailed explanation and determine the minimum breakdown voltage.
2. Working mechanism. I find the working mechanism proposed in this paper quite perplexing. Conventional avalanche devices rely on “junctions” to establish strong electric fields, thereby accelerating carriers and enabling the avalanche multiplication process through impact ionization. Recently, some studies (e.g. Nat. Nanotechnol. 2019, 14, 217-222; Nature Communications 2024, 15, 3639) have achieved localized electric fields and reduced scattering by constructing novel structures, such as vertical junctions or van der Waals stepwise homojunctions, leading to lower avalanche threshold voltages. Given these considerations, I have two questions:
1) The proposed structure in this work lacks junction-induced localized electric fields (as the authors stated in Supplementary Figure 2d), which are typically crucial for avalanche multiplication, yet it achieves a relatively low avalanche threshold voltage compared to conventional designs. Could the authors provide further explanations in light of recent literature (e.g. Nat. Nanotechnol. 2019, 14, 217-222; Nature Communications 2024, 15, 3639)? Additionally, what is the electric field distribution within the proposed device structure? Could the authors support their findings using TCAD simulations—a widely accepted theoretical approach in previous studies—to validate the proposed avalanche multiplication mechanism?
2) According to the avalanche mechanism proposed by the authors, since both terminals form ohmic contacts with the material, the two electrodes should be electrically equivalent. Therefore, shouldn't the device exhibit symmetric I-V characteristics and avalanche multiplication processes under bidirectional bias? Specifically, when the left terminal is grounded, avalanche multiplication should theoretically occur under both positive and negative bias applied to the right terminal. The authors should provide complete I-V characteristics spanning from negative to positive bias, such as the -5V to +5V range in Figure 2a, to demonstrate this symmetry.
3. Gate Voltage Modulation Characteristics. The authors present the breakdown voltage versus gate voltage curve in Figure 2. Here, I have two questions:
1) Negative Gate Bias Dependence: As the gate voltage becomes more negative, does the breakdown voltage continue to decrease? What is the minimum achievable breakdown voltage (i.e., the performance limit of the breakdown voltage)?
2) Positive Gate Bias Dependence: How does the breakdown voltage behave when the gate voltage is increased in the positive direction? Does it exhibit saturation, increase, or an unexpected trend?
To strengthen the credibility of the findings, the authors should provide extended gate voltage sweep data, covering both deeper negative and positive bias regimes. This would help clarify the full gate-dependent breakdown behavior and validate the proposed mechanism.
4. Rate of increase in the current. The authors have not fully addressed my previous question (Q1 from the first round of review). They should provide a comprehensive comparison of the I-V characteristics between ReSe and commercial devices (such as InGaAs, Si, etc. Hamamatsu G8931 series. https://www.hamamatsu.com.cn/cn/zh-cn/product/optical-sensors/apd/ingaas-apd/G8931-04.html), with particular focus on extracting the avalanche current rise rate (dVds/dlog(Ids)). In conventional devices like InGaAs APDs, the avalanche current rise rate typically exceeds 400 mV/dec. This quantitative comparison represents a critical benchmark for assessing avalanche performance, as originally highlighted in Reviewer #1’s comments (Q4). The authors must rigorously address this fundamental issue to validate their claims regarding avalanche current.

In the revised manuscript, while the authors have addressed some of the previous points, major concerns persist regarding several critical issues, notably the identification of the avalanche mechanism and the origin of the dark current. I have serious reservations on these points, which I believe constitute fundamental flaws that could easily lead to significant misinterpretation of the results. My specific comments are as follows:
(1) In connection with the dark current issue (Q1) I raised in the previous review round, I still have concerns. While I appreciate your effort to clarify the temperature-dependent behavior of the dark current in the linear region of your ReSe₂ FET, I find the explanation provided still unsatisfactory and inconsistent with your own experimental data.
You argue that the increase in dark current with decreasing temperature is due to a mobility increase that outweighs the change in carrier density. However, your extracted mobility values from Supplementary Fig. 15a show only a minor change (<10%) in the temperature range above 200 K. In contrast, the dark current in Supplementary Fig. 3d increases by several times over the same temperature range. This significant discrepancy clearly contradicts your proposed mechanism and suggests that the mobility change alone cannot account for the pronounced increase in dark current.
Moreover, I remain deeply concerned about the presentation of your results. As a study on an avalanche photodiode (APD), it is essential to include temperature-dependent characterizations-especially those related to dark current-in the main text, rather than relegating them to the Supplementary Materials. The temperature dependence of key parameters is central to the understanding of avalanche mechanisms and device performance. Its omission from the main text severely limits the readers’ ability to evaluate the validity and novelty of your claims.
(2) Regarding the relationship between avalanche threshold voltage and temperature (Q2) that I raised in the previous review round, I still have concerns. In the last review, I pointed out that the breakdown voltage drops sharply from approximately 2 V to 1.4 V when the temperature decreases from 300 K to 280 K (a mere 20 K variation). The authors attributed this discrepancy to the fact that "the 300 K data and the low-temperature data were taken months apart." I find this explanation highly unsatisfactory, as all data should ideally be collected in a single, continuous measurement session to ensure consistency. Presenting data acquired under such inconsistent conditions may easily mislead readers.
I appreciate that the authors have addressed this issue by re-measuring the same device in one day using a continuous temperature sweep from 300 K down to 77 K (as shown in Supplementary Fig. 3d). However, I regret to say that the new data still appear insufficient to support definitive conclusions. First, although the figure caption mentions I-V curves at nine temperature points from 300 K to 77 K, only seven curves are actually displayed-data for 160 K and 100 K are missing. Second, I have reservations about how the threshold voltage was determined. While the authors describe the extraction method in Supplementary Section “5. Avalanche breakdown voltage (Vb) extraction,” the procedure applied in Fig. 3b does not seem fully consistent with this description. For instance, the data at 220 K and 120 K appear nearly identical, yet the extracted threshold voltages (Supplementary Fig. 3e) differ by approximately 0.3 V. These issues raise concerns about the validity of the data.
(3) In Figure 4, the authors present the optoelectronic performance characterization. I find this part of the analysis lacking in professionalism.
i) Firstly, calculating D* solely based on dark current (Idark) may introduce significant errors. It is important to note that the dark current (Ids) is primarily influenced by shot noise. The photogain (avalanche gain) should be considered when calculating the detectivity (D*), as the noise current will also be amplified by the gain, which is approximately 173 in this work. Additionally, thermal noise and generation-recombination noise-two significant sources of noise-appear to have been overlooked. I recommend testing the noise current using standard methods (e.g., Nature, 2017, 542, 324) before recalculating the detectivity;
ii) Please use the international units "cm Hz^1/2 W^-1" for detectivity;
iii) The decay time should be presented as a data point plot. Furthermore, the testing method and definition of response time should be clearly specified in the article.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: Throughout the revision, the authors have made significant efforts to address many of my concerns.
